messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Dr. Marcos Delgado

Dr. Marcos Delgado was forty years old and had been a trauma surgeon for fifteen years when the earthquake struck Port-au-Prince on the morning of January 12, 2010. He had been there for a medical mission, part of a rotating group of volunteer surgeons from Miami who spent two weeks at a time providing pro bono care at a rural clinic in the hills outside the capital. Marcos had always been drawn to this work—his parents had emigrated from Puerto Rico with nothing, and he felt a deep obligation to give back to communities that reminded him of the stories they told about their own struggles. He was in the surgical tent when the ground began to move, a sensation he would later struggle to articulate to his wife, Rosa. It wasn't just shaking; it was the earth itself seeming to liquefy beneath his feet, the canvas walls of the tent collapsing inward like a lung deflating. He remembered the sound most vividly—not the roar everyone spoke of, but the specific high-pitched screech of metal supports twisting, a sound that seemed to split his skull open. Then came the dust, thick and acrid, coating his mouth and throat with the taste of concrete and something else, something burnt that he couldn't identify. He had clawed his way out from under collapsed shelving, his hands bleeding, and spent the next thirty-six hours working in the rubble alongside other survivors, operating by candlelight on injuries he could barely see, amputating limbs, pronouncing people dead when their injuries were beyond salvage. He had never fully remembered the sequence of those hours—there were gaps, blank stretches where he must have done things but could not reconstruct them, as if his mind had simply stopped recording.

When Marcos returned to Miami three weeks later, he threw himself back into his routine at Jackson Memorial Hospital, telling Rosa and his two teenage children that he was fine, that he had processed what he'd seen, that he was grateful to have survived when so many hadn't. For the first few months, this felt almost true. But by late spring, his body had begun to betray him. Loud noises—the crash of a surgical tray, a car backfiring on the street, even the unexpected slam of a door—would send him into a state of hypervigilance that lasted for hours. His hands would shake, his heart would race, and for a moment the operating room would dissolve and he would be back in that tent, searching for people who were no longer there. The smell of smoke was worse. During a routine fire drill at the hospital that June, he had smelled the training smoke and found himself unable to move, unable to breathe, standing frozen in a hallway while colleagues passed him with concern in their eyes. He had called in sick for three days after that, claiming a migraine.

By autumn, Marcos had developed a pattern of coping that felt necessary, even logical, though he recognized on some level that it was spiraling. He drank most evenings—a glass of whiskey, sometimes two or three, which he told himself was no different from what many of his colleagues did. He had begun to use alcohol more deliberately, timing his drinks to coincide with the hours when his mind was most likely to drift toward the memories he couldn't fully grasp, the missing pieces that haunted him precisely because he couldn't see them. He had also discovered that sexual activity with Rosa—or increasingly, fantasies engaged in alone—provided a temporary relief, a way to redirect the physical tension that seemed to accumulate in his body throughout the day. Rosa had noticed the change in his desire, initially pleased, then confused and eventually withdrawn when she sensed something mechanical in his approach. He had also become expert at distraction: he would immerse himself in work, staying late at the hospital, taking on extra cases, filling every moment with tasks that required his complete attention. When that wasn't possible, he would scroll through his phone for hours, watching videos, reading news, anything to keep his mind from settling into the spaces where the memories lived.

What had finally forced him to seek help was an incident three months ago. During a routine laparoscopic surgery, a monitor had emitted a high-pitched alert—a common sound, nothing unusual. But something in its frequency had triggered a flash of the screech from the tent, and Marcos had lost focus completely. His hands had stilled. For perhaps five seconds, he had been somewhere else entirely, and when he returned to himself, he found his attending surgeon looking at him with unmistakable alarm. Nothing had gone wrong—his hands had been steady enough that no harm came to the patient—but the message was clear: his ability to function at the level his patients deserved was deteriorating. Rosa had noticed his drinking intensifying in the weeks after. She had found him one night in their garage with a bottle of mezcal, and when she asked him what was happening, he had broken down in a way he hadn't since returning from Haiti, telling her about the gaps in his memory, about the way grief would crash over him without warning when something—a smell, a sound, a moment of stillness—brought the event back. He was certain that his mind was fragmenting, that he was losing pieces of himself he would never recover. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, but the ones he couldn't access, the sense that he had survived something so catastrophic that his own mind had refused to record it. He had called his employee assistance program the next morning, and now, sitting in the waiting room of a therapist's office, Marcos was holding onto the hope that someone could help him understand what his mind had taken from him, and whether he could ever trust himself in the operating room again.
